hazards.chase-door: You went out the door after them. Once the till is in their hands the robbery is over; a bartender chasing an armed stranger into a parking lot alone is a second, voluntary crime scene, and the description you can give standing still is worth more than one given from a hospital bed.
hazards.reach-weapon: You reached for the bat kept under the register. Nothing behind this bar is worth a physical confrontation, and a weapon raised at a robber is what turns a compliant hand-over into a shooting — the whole policy exists to take that choice off the table before it is ever offered.
hazards.solo-carry: You took the deposit out through the back hallway alone instead of waiting for your escort. The whole reason two people walk a drop is that one bartender carrying a bank bag across an empty room is the easiest target in the building — the escort is the control, not the paperwork after it.
hazards.torn-bag: You sealed the deposit in the torn bag sitting by the register instead of a fresh one. A bag that has already been opened proves nothing if the count is ever questioned — the tamper strip is the only evidence that nobody touched it between the drawer and the safe.

interrupts.alert: A regular has leaned right over the service rail and is watching you count the drawer, bill by bill.
interrupts.cue: Close it up, or finish the count where they can't see it.
interrupts.missNote: You kept counting in full view of the rail. The count itself came out fine; what left the building tonight was a stranger's read on how much cash was in your hands and roughly when it would be moving.
interrupts.why: A customer who has watched a full till count now knows roughly how much cash is in the building and about when it moves — closing the drawer, or finishing the count out of sight in the office, removes that information before it becomes anybody's plan.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the drawer. Close it, or take the count where the rail can't see it — that is the whole response here.

interrupts.alert: Your colleague has wedged the back door open for a smoke break while you're mid-walk with the deposit still in your hands.
interrupts.cue: Shut and secure it before you take another step.
interrupts.missNote: The back door stayed open for the rest of the walk. An unsecured entry point during a drop is exactly the kind of gap a robbery gets planned around, propped by accident or not.
interrupts.why: A propped door during a cash move is an open entry point timed to the one moment the building's cash is actually exposed and moving. It gets shut immediately, the walk finishes, and the smoke break waits five more minutes.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the back door. Shut and secure it — the walk to the safe can wait the three seconds that takes.

lateNotes.front-deadbolt: The door gets locked once the robber is clear of it, not before — a locked door mid-robbery traps everyone inside with them.
lateNotes.panic-button: The alarm gets pressed after they've left, not while they're still at the counter — trip it now and a compliant hand-over can turn into a hostage situation.
lateNotes.violence-log-sheet: The log gets written after the drawer, the alarm and the call — not instead of any of them.

name: Till Drop & Robbery Response

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Page a second staff member — the count does not start alone.
steps.prompt: Page a second staff member — the count does not start alone.
steps.title: Call a witness before you open the drawer
steps.why: A till count with only one set of eyes on it is one person's word against a shortage that shows up later. UNITE HERE Local 2's cash-handling language and ordinary loss-prevention practice both start the same way: a second person present, so the number on the sheet is a fact two people watched happen.

steps.cue: Hold the count steady — the drawer stays open only as long as counting takes.
steps.holdBreakNote: You broke off mid-count with the drawer still open. Start the count again — an interrupted count with an open drawer is the exact window this procedure exists to close.
steps.prompt: Hold the count steady — the drawer stays open only as long as counting takes.
steps.title: Count the drawer down
steps.why: The drawer is at its most exposed the moment it is open and being counted, so the count itself is done fast and covered — hands moving the whole time, nobody outside the till involved, and the drawer shut the instant the total is confirmed.

steps.cue: Run the terminal's batch close and commit when it lands on the settlement total.

gauge.label: BATCH $
gauge.missNote: Off the settlement total — the terminal and the paper tape do not agree yet. Run the batch again before it's filed.

steps.prompt: Run the terminal's batch close and commit when it lands on the settlement total.
steps.title: Reconcile the card batch to the settlement total
steps.why: The batch total on the terminal and the printed receipts have to land on the same number tonight, not at month's end — a card run twice, declined, or refunded wrong is a two-minute fix at close and a chargeback dispute with the processor a month later.

steps.cue: Write the total first, then seal the envelope.
steps.outOfOrderNote: The total gets written down before the envelope is sealed — a sealed envelope with no record behind it is a number nobody can check later.
steps.prompt: Write the total first, then seal the envelope.
steps.title: Record and seal the tip-out
steps.why: California Labor Code §351 makes a tip the employee's property the moment it is earned, which is exactly why it is counted and written down before it is ever divided or sealed — the record is what makes a split provable instead of just assumed.

steps.cue: Fresh bag, logged serial number, sealed in front of your witness.
steps.prompt: Fresh bag, logged serial number, sealed in front of your witness.
steps.title: Seal the deposit in a fresh tamper-evident bag
steps.why: A tamper-evident bag with a logged serial number is the only thing that can prove later that nobody opened the deposit between the drawer and the bank. A bag that is not sealed, or is not fresh, proves nothing either way.

steps.cue: Steady, unhurried pace to the safe — not a stroll, not a sprint.
steps.holdBreakNote: Pace drifted out of band. Dawdling leaves the cash exposed longer than it needs to be; rushing is how a sealed bag ends up dropped on the floor.
steps.prompt: Steady, unhurried pace to the safe — not a stroll, not a sprint.
steps.title: Walk the drop with your escort
steps.why: Two people walking a cash drop is the whole control, not a courtesy. A single bartender crossing an empty bar with the night's deposit is the easiest robbery in the building to plan around, and the escort beside you is what removes that opportunity entirely.

steps.cue: Carry it to the drop slot and set it in — nowhere else along the way.

drag.missNote: Not lined up with the drop slot. A bag set down beside the safe is a bag that is not in the safe.

steps.prompt: Carry it to the drop slot and set it in — nowhere else along the way.
steps.title: Put the bag straight into the safe
steps.why: The bag goes straight into the safe's slot, not set down on a counter or a shelf along the way. Every second it spends anywhere else is a second it is not secured, in a room with someone who has no reason to be walking behind you.

steps.cue: Time, amount, and both sets of initials.
steps.prompt: Time, amount, and both sets of initials.
steps.title: Log the drop
steps.why: Time, amount, and both sets of initials in the drop log turn 'we made a drop' into a record the manager, the bank reconciliation, and — if it is ever needed — an investigator can all check against each other.

steps.cue: Hands visible, open the drawer, hand it over. Hold steady.
steps.holdBreakNote: You pulled back mid-hand-over. A hesitation here reads as resistance to someone who is already keyed up — keep it slow, visible and steady until the till is in their hands.
steps.prompt: Hands visible, open the drawer, hand it over. Hold steady.
steps.title: A demand for the till — comply
steps.why: Nothing behind this counter is worth a life, and the till is insured — every dollar in it replaceable in a way a bartender's or a customer's safety is not. Compliance is fast, it is quiet, and it ends the encounter sooner than anything else that has ever been tried instead.

steps.cue: Note the direction, the build, the clothing. Stay behind the bar.
steps.prompt: Note the direction, the build, the clothing. Stay behind the bar.
steps.title: Watch them leave — do not follow
steps.why: Once the till leaves the counter the robbery is over, and a foot chase is a separate, voluntary decision to follow an armed stranger into a place with no witnesses and no backup. A description given standing still is worth more to police than one given from an ambulance.

steps.cue: Press it after the door closes behind them, not before.
steps.prompt: Press it after the door closes behind them, not before.
steps.title: Silent alarm — once they're gone
steps.why: The alarm is pressed once they are gone, not while they are still in the room — a silent alarm that stops being silent because it is tripped mid-robbery can turn a compliant hand-over into an armed standoff nobody chose to have.

steps.cue: Bolt the front door the moment they're clear of it.
steps.prompt: Bolt the front door the moment they're clear of it.
steps.title: Lock the door behind them
steps.why: Locking the door the moment the robber is clear keeps the scene the way it was left — no new customer wandering in across a shoeprint or a dropped shell casing before police have had a chance to see either one.

steps.cue: Direction of travel, description, weapon if any — while it's fresh.
steps.prompt: Direction of travel, description, weapon if any — while it's fresh.
steps.title: Call 911
steps.why: Police need the description, the direction they left in, and the weapon if any while all three are still fresh in your head, not after the doors are swept and the register is quietly reopened for the next round of customers.

steps.cue: Nobody touches the counter. Pull and save the camera footage before the loop overwrites it.

itemNotes.cctv-save: The DVR's own loop will overwrite tonight's footage in days unless it's pulled and saved before that happens.
itemNotes.no-touch-zone: Fingerprints and the counter surface are evidence, and every hand that touches it after the fact is a print police now have to rule out.

steps.prompt: Nobody touches the counter. Pull and save the camera footage before the loop overwrites it.
steps.title: Preserve the scene and the footage
steps.why: Fingerprints, the counter surface, and the camera footage are the case, and every one of them degrades the longer people move through the space. The counter stays untouched and the footage is pulled and saved before the system's own loop erases it for good.

steps.cue: Write it up while it's fresh — this is the record the plan gets reviewed against.
steps.prompt: Write it up while it's fresh — this is the record the plan gets reviewed against.
steps.title: File the Cal/OSHA workplace-violence log entry
steps.why: Cal/OSHA's workplace violence prevention plan (8 CCR §3342, from SB 553) requires every incident like this one logged — not as paperwork after the fact, but as the record the next safety-committee review and the next OSHA inspection both draw on to change what happens before the next one.

tagline: Count the till with a witness, drop it with an escort, and if someone demands the drawer instead: comply, don't chase, alarm after they're gone, lock up, call 911, and log it
